item.title: California Dems trigger outrage after siding with convicted child sex offenders in shocking vote
item.description: California Senate Democrats rejected a Republican effort to ban all sex offender registry tiers from holding public office, including school board seats, in a party-line vote.
item.content:encoded:
California Senate Democrats rejected Republican Sen. Suzette Valladares’ effort to close a "loophole" allowing some people convicted of sex crimes against minors to seek public office, including school-board seats.

At issue is AB 2691, a proposal to add sexual assault and human trafficking to the felony convictions that disqualify Californians from elected office. Valladares’ amendment sought to undo Democratic-led changes that allow people convicted of certain sex crimes against minors to remain eligible to seek public office.

"Right now in California, someone convicted of sexually abusing a child can still sit on your school board. That's not a loophole. That's a choice. And in my perspective, and most, that's wrong," Valladares, R-Santa Clarita, said on the California Senate floor while urging colleagues to adopt an amendment that Senate Democrats later rejected on a party-line vote, according to her office. 

"Predators who sexually abuse children have no place holding public office. None, not in the Capitol, not on city council, and definitely not on our school boards. AB 2691 was supposed to guarantee that. It started as a simple ban," she continued. "Convicted sex offenders don't get to hold public office. Period. But amendments added this summer gutted it, narrowing the bill to cover only tier three offenders and deliberately exempting tier one and tier two."

SEX CRIMES COULD COST LAWMAKERS TAXPAYER-FUNDED PENSIONS UNDER HAWLEY’S NEW PROPOSAL

Under the bill’s current language, the new public-office ban would apply to sexual-assault convictions requiring lifetime Tier 3 sex-offender registration. People whose convictions place them in Tier 1 or Tier 2 — categories requiring at least 10 or 20 years on the registry before they can ask a court for removal — would not be disqualified under the proposed law.

Concern was also raised months ago during a Senate committee hearing, when Republican California state Sen. Steven Choi asked Assemblywoman Dawn Addis, the bill’s Democratic author, why people convicted of certain sex crimes against minors could remain eligible to seek office under the amended measure. Addis did not address the specific offenses Choi identified, instead calling AB 2691 a "first in the nation" proposal that would protect survivors and saying she was open to working with lawmakers on other crimes.

"We're doing a first in the nation bill that would protect the public trust of survivors and would make sure that survivors are really in the lead," Addis responded. "Happy to continue working with the committee or others if there are other kinds of crimes folks feel need to be addressed. But at the moment, I feel like we have a really important bill that is nation leading, that will uplift survivors and enhance public trust here in California."

DRAG QUEEN SCHOOL BOARD VICE PRESIDENT ARRESTED ON CHILD PORNOGRAPHY AND ENDANGERMENT CHARGES

California state Sen. Scott Wiener, the Democratic chair of the committee that considered the bill, argued that a broader prohibition based on all three registry tiers would be overbroad. He said California’s registry had historically included both "sexually violent predator[s]" and others who have committed less serious crimes, citing an example of "a gay guy who had sex in a park or in a car and got arrested."

"Sex offender registry is not punishment," Wiener argued. "It is a tool for law enforcement to be able to monitor people who may potentially cause a risk. And when we use the sex offender registry as a proxy for anything else, we get into problems."

But Sen. Valladares told Fox News Digital that the issue "isn't complicated" for her.

"I’m a mom. This one isn’t complicated for me. Today, 40 senators had the chance to say convicted sex offenders should NEVER hold public office in California," she told Fox News Digital. "Ten Republicans stood up to vote for what is right. My amendments would have closed the door. No loopholes. No exceptions. No convicted sex offenders serving in positions of public trust, including on our school boards. Protecting our kids should NEVER be partisan. I’m deeply disappointed, and I’m not done fighting."

item.title: WNBA coach leaves it to the league to handle transgender eligibility issue amid mounting criticism
item.description: Nate Tibbetts deferred to the WNBA league office on the transgender eligibility policy after Charles Barkley criticized Adam Silver and Cathy Engelbert.
item.content:encoded:
Phoenix Mercury head coach Nate Tibbetts said Tuesday night it’s up to the league office when it comes to the WNBA’s transgender eligibility policy as the league faced criticism from Charles Barkley.

Barkley, a Basketball Hall of Famer and former Phoenix Suns star, said on a podcast earlier this week he was "disappointed in Adam Silver and Cathy Engelbert" for failing to nip the transgender athlete issue in the bud when they had the chance.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

OutKick asked Tibbetts about Barkley’s comments before Phoenix’s 94-84 loss to the Washington Mystics.

"Yeah, I’m going to leave that to the league office," Tibbetts said. "That’s their job. We’re here to play a basketball game here tonight."

OutKick asked the WNBA and NBA for a reaction to Tibbetts’ comments but has yet to hear back.

The WNBA’s eligibility policy is opaque at best. The league’s collective bargaining agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." However, it doesn’t include specific language on whether players who are born male and identify as female could compete in the league. Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White have since declared their intentions to enter the WNBA Draft.

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert denounced those she claimed are trying to "sow divisiveness" over the transgender issue.

"People are trying to use the league to sow divisiveness," Engelbert said earlier this month.

"We're being the center of political football for people who have never watched the WNBA, never have written about the WNBA or reported on the WNBA."

item.title: ‘Captain Canada’ firebrand unloads on Trump with profane one-liner as trade war escalates
item.description: Ontario Premier Doug Ford told President Donald Trump to "kiss my as*" on CP24 after Trump mocked him as less impressive than late brother Rob Ford.
item.content:encoded:
A simmering trade rift between President Donald Trump and Canadian officials burst into the open Monday as Ontario premier Doug Ford sharply escalated his attacks on the president amid a widening tariff fight between the longtime allies.

"He can kiss my a– as far as I’m concerned. We’re going to go at him full steam, and we buy 400% more cars than anyone in the world," Ford said in an interview with Toronto radio station Newstalk 1010 Monday in response to Trump’s threat of new tariffs on Canadian autos, auto parts and steel.

Trump mocked Ford on Monday as "less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive" than his late brother, former Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, who became embroiled in a major 2013 scandal over his use of crack cocaine, which he later admitted.

The Ontario premier, dubbed "Captain Canada," has since emerged as one of the country’s most outspoken critics of Trump’s trade threats.

TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS

The tariff fight is unfolding on two tracks: new 50% U.S. tariffs on certain Canadian goods took effect Aug. 22, with Canada set to retaliate Sept. 8, while Trump separately threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian autos and auto parts to 50% beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

The White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump’s Truth Social posts when approached for additional comment. 

"America has been carrying Canada for decades, but no longer! The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada. Without the United States, Canada couldn’t survive — It’s where they get all of their money and, because of their current bad leadership, primarily Governor Carney, and his Flunky, Ford, they will not be allowed to keep taking advantage of the United States — Their key to survival," Trump added in a post.

TRUMP MUST CLOSE THE BACK DOOR CHINA USES TO EXPLOIT NORTH AMERICAN TRADE

He claimed Canada imposes tariffs of 400% or more on U.S. farmers and said he plans to end what he describes as unfair trade treatment of American companies and producers. Trump also threatened further economic pressure, claiming much of the electricity, oil and gas Canada receives is transported through the U.S. and calling on the country to "fall in line."

CANADA REPORTEDLY SCRAPS JOINT BRIDGE CELEBRATION WITH US AFTER TRUMP RENEWS TARIFF THREAT

Beyond tariffs, Trump also escalated the rhetoric Tuesday by floating a proposal to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America."

The current tariff fight traces back to late 2024, when Trump threatened 25% tariffs on Canadian goods and later joked during a meeting with then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau that Canada could become the 51st state.

Fox News Digital reached out to Ford for comment.

item.title: The left’s constitutional hypocrisy is on full display in its war on Trump
item.description: Trump's resistance to judicial rulings on birthright citizenship and tariffs echoes Jefferson, Lincoln and Roosevelt's departmentalist tradition.
item.content:encoded:
Progressives have spent months insisting that President Trump is "ignoring the rule of law" whenever he resists or questions judicial rulings — on birthright citizenship, trade policy, the removal of Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, or even the addition of his name to the Kennedy Center. The critique collapses under the weight of the Left’s own constitutional commitments. Many of the same people attacking Trump champion popular constitutionalism and departmentalism — two frameworks that explicitly reject judicial supremacy and affirm the independent interpretive authority of the elected branches.

In today’s hyper‑ politicized legal environment, the Left’s selective outrage obscures the constitutional reality.

Popular constitutionalism, most famously explicated by former Stanford Law dean Larry Kramer in The People Themselves, holds that the people — acting through elected officials — retain ultimate authority over constitutional meaning. Courts are not supreme; they are participants in a broader constitutional conversation. Departmentalism, embraced by presidents from Thomas Jefferson to Richard Nixon, similarly maintains that each branch has an independent duty to interpret the Constitution.

GORSUCH SAYS IDEOLOGICAL DIVIDES ON SUPREME COURT COME DOWN TO ‘HOW YOU READ LAW,’ NOT POLITICS

Crucially, departmentalism draws a distinction modern critics ignore: while a court’s judgment binds specific parties in a specific case, it does not bind the political branches as a permanent mandate. Rejecting judicial supremacy is not defying the rule of law; it is rejecting the idea that five or six judges have a monopoly on constitutional truth. That view is a mainstream critique of judicial supremacy, yet when Trump invokes the same logic, the Left treats departmentalism as dangerous heresy.

Trump’s critics speak as though presidential resistance to judicial interpretations is unprecedented, but it is woven into American history. Thomas Jefferson refused to treat Marbury v. Madison as binding beyond the parties, writing that "each of the three departments has equally the right to decide for itself what is its duty under the Constitution." Andrew Jackson declared the Supreme Court’s views "ought not to control the coordinate authorities of this government." Abraham Lincoln treated Dred Scott v. Sandford as binding only on the immediate litigants, refusing to accept it as a permanent rule for the nation. Franklin Roosevelt openly challenged the Court’s constitutional interpretations during the New Deal, and Richard Nixon frequently asserted independent executive authority in administrative matters. If presidential resistance to judicial supremacy were inherently lawless, half of America’s most consequential presidents would be guilty of it.

LIBERAL STATE SUPREME COURT JUSTICE BLASTS SCOTUS CONSERVATIVES, SAYS HAWAII WILL DEFY HIGH COURT

Trump’s actions fall squarely within this tradition. Much of today’s friction stems not from executive defiance of individual decrees, but from lower courts relying on nationwide injunctions that attempt to freeze executive action everywhere at once. That modern dynamic makes departmentalist principles more relevant than ever. The Supreme Court’s recent jurisprudence has pushed back against such injunctions, emphasizing that lower courts exceed their constitutional authority when they attempt to issue sweeping rules binding the entire government. That judicial self‑restraint aligns directly with departmentalism: the judiciary’s role is to resolve specific disputes between specific litigants, not to govern coequal branches.

Critics point to Trump’s continuing efforts to end birthright citizenship as proof of lawlessness. But the dispute is fundamentally about constitutional interpretation. Although the Supreme Court recently ruled against Trump’s position, pressing the argument again through distinct legal channels reflects the same iterative process past presidents used when they believed the Court misread the Constitution.

TRUMP CRITICIZES 2 SUPREME COURT JUSTICES BY NAME OVER TARIFF RULING

The same dynamic defines recent tariff disputes. When the Supreme Court ruled in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not delegate unilateral tariff-setting authority, the administration’s pivot to alternative statutory mechanisms was labeled lawlessness. But testing other delegations passed by Congress is standard interbranch dialogue.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The rule of law does not require presidents to treat judicial interpretations as infallible. It requires them to operate within constitutional limits — and assert their own constitutional judgments when appropriate. President Trump is doing exactly that.

This isn’t an abstract point for me. Long before Donald Trump entered national politics, I wrote a book published by Oxford University Press making the historical case against popular constitutionalism and departmentalism — an originalist defense of judicial finality. But that scholarly position does not mean President Trump is ignoring the rule of law or behaving like an authoritarian when he advances a theory of judicial review that other presidents and scholars have likewise advanced.

The real danger is not presidential resistance to judicial supremacy — it is the selective outrage that turns constitutional theory into a partisan weapon.

item.title: The bravest Jews in America are 15 years old — and they’re going back to school
item.description: Every August American parents add new worries to back-to-school lists, but Jewish Student Union teens are building community instead of hiding identity.
item.content:encoded:
Every August, American parents make back-to-school lists. Notebooks. Sneakers. A new backpack.

For many Jewish parents, another set of questions has joined that list. Should my daughter wear her Star of David, or tuck it inside her shirt? Should my son keep the Israeli flag sticker on his water bottle, or peel it off? When my kid asks for days off for Rosh Hashanah so early in the semester, how will the teacher respond?

I lead Jewish Student Union, a national network of more than 515 clubs serving over 21,000 Jewish teens in public and community high schools across the United States and Canada. Before Oct. 7, 2023, we estimate that we received roughly 15 to 20 requests a year from teens looking to start new JSU clubs. Since then, 473 teens have sought us out through our national system to request a club at their school. And that number captures only the teens who found us on their own. It doesn’t include teens who already know a local JSU staff member through community programming or a summer experience or who hear about JSU from a friend at another school and reach out directly.

EXTREMISM THRIVES IN 'KEYBOARD COURTROOM' — AMERICA MUST THINK LIKE JURORS, NOT MOBS

What those club requests tell me is that at a moment when being Jewish can feel complicated and even ostracizing, teens aren’t asking for less Judaism. They’re asking for more opportunities to find one another, build the Jewish community and take an active role in shaping it.

That desire for Jewish community is especially meaningful given the environment many of these teens are navigating. In Michigan, for example, Jewish students are heading back to school after a particularly difficult year for their community. In March, a terrorist attacked the largest synagogue in the state in Bloomfield Hills. 

And a few weeks ago, Michigan Democrats nominated Abdul El-Sayed for the U.S. Senate — a candidate who called the Israeli government just as "evil" as Hamas and has publicly questioned whether Israel should exist as a Jewish state. The Anti-Defamation League — an organization that almost never wades into campaigns — called him out by name for peddling antisemitic tropes.

Now imagine you're a Jewish sophomore at a public high school in Ann Arbor or West Bloomfield. You're watching these debates unfold in your own community while navigating the ordinary challenges of being a teenager. Conversations about Israel and Jewish identity don't stay confined to political campaigns or university campuses. They make their way into social media feeds, conversations with classmates and school hallways.

Adults spend a great deal of time worrying about how young Jews will respond to this moment. From my vantage point, I have the privilege of seeing their response every day.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

These teens aren’t hiding their Judaism to survive high school. They’re deepening it. Starting Jewish communities in their schools. Showing up for Shabbat dinners. Learning about Israel and traveling there. Displaying their Star of David necklaces proudly.

This summer, a senior in New Jersey transferred from a public high school with an active JSU club to a school without one. She could have simply left that part of her high school experience behind. Instead, she reached out to her former JSU adviser and asked for his help starting a club at her new school. She recruited her younger brother and sister, another senior and that student’s younger sister. Before school even began, they sat down with their JSU advisor to plan for the club fair, talk through leadership roles and brainstorm club activities.

Each came with a different reason for wanting JSU at their school. One wanted to help their peers see Jews and Judaism in a positive light. Another wanted more opportunities to learn about Judaism. A third wanted to create a space where Jewish students could feel safe and connected without everything becoming political.

Together, they began building the Jewish community they wanted to have at their school. And their JSU adviser will be there with them every week, with kosher food, engaging activities, Torah insights and, most importantly, a relationship they can count on.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That relationship is at the heart of Jewish engagement. Across JSU, staff get to know teens as individuals, show up consistently in their lives and create spaces where they can ask questions, explore their Judaism and figure out what it means to them. A club may gather in a classroom during lunchtime, but those relationships extend far beyond a weekly meeting — into after-school programs, Shabbat dinners, volunteering opportunities, summer experiences and the many moments in between.

After two decades in Jewish education, I've learned that you can't tell a teenager to care about being Jewish. You have to give them opportunities to discover why it matters to them. That happens through relationships. Through community. Through experiences that allow Judaism to become something they live and choose for themselves.

Those foundations matter in every generation. At a moment when being openly Jewish can feel more complicated, they matter even more.

This back-to-school season, I have a request for every adult reading this. To principals and school boards: protect your Jewish students' right to gather, express their identity and build community as fiercely as you would for any other group of students. To parents: pay attention to what your teen is experiencing as a Jewish student. Ask questions, listen and make sure they know they have somewhere to turn. And to the Jewish community: don't assume that this generation is pulling away. Give them opportunities to belong, people who will invest in them and experiences that allow them to discover what being Jewish means to them.

The bravest Jews in America don't hold office. Some of them are 15 years old, gathering their friends around a table at lunch and choosing to build Jewish community where none existed before.

This September, they'll walk through their school doors with their heads held high. Our job is to make sure they never have to walk through them alone.

item.title: Dolly Parton's life in her own words: from Smoky Mountains poverty to country music immortality
item.description: Dolly Parton's life in her own words reveals her Smoky Mountains childhood, faith, marriage to Carl Dean and her views on aging and what comes after.
item.content:encoded:
Country music icon Dolly Parton died peacefully in Nashville on Tuesday at 80 years old. Parton's team shared a statement with Fox News Digital on Tuesday night and confirmed that she died after a "brief battle with cancer."

Parton's death sparked mourning across the world. Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard."

Throughout the span of her career, which ignited as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," Parton always shared what mattered most to her – her Tennessee upbringing, her faith, her beloved husband, Carl Dean, and family.

Below is a look at Parton's life, in her own words, over the years.

DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80

Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child and started writing songs at a young age.

In 2015, Parton told Entertainment Tonight that her upbringing shaped who she became in her adult years. "I think my childhood made me everything I am today. I would trade nothing for being brought up in the Great Smoky Mountains. I’ve never been ashamed of my people no matter how poor or dirty we might have been," she said at the time.

Parton added, "I’ve always loved being from where I am, and having the folks that I’ve had."

During an interview with Rolling Stone in January, Parton shed a little more light on her poor childhood and said that her mother would make her clothes out of "feed sacks or scraps."

"We didn’t have anything. Mama used to sew all of our quilts and curtains for the windows, remake our clothes, and make clothes out of feed sacks or scraps," she said.

Parton was one of 12 children. Her parents were Robert Lee Parton Sr., known as Lee, a sharecropper and construction worker, and Avie Lee Caroline Parton, who raised their family.

Parton was very outspoken throughout her life about her Christian faith. During an interview with Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that her faith impacted everything she did.

GRAMMY-NOMINATED SINGER ANNE WILSON SAYS SPEAKING ABOUT JESUS COST HER OPPORTUNITIES, BUT SHE WON'T BACK DOWN

"My faith impacts everything I do because I do believe that, through God, all things are possible," she said at the time. "I always ask God to bless everything that I do and the people that I work with and to bring all the right things and right people into my life and to take the wrong ones out."

WATCH: Dolly Parton discusses the important role faith plays in her life

She added, "My spirituality has been a guiding light in my life and my strength, really, in my creative energy."

On the WorkLife with Adam Grant Ted Talk series in 2022, Parton shared that her religious beliefs were instilled in her at a young age.

"My grandpa was preacher. My mom was very religious, very spiritual. So I learned all the good lessons about loving your neighbor as yourself and judge not lest you be judged. Through God, all things are possible," she said.

WILLIE ROBERTSON'S FAITH-BASED ADVICE THAT'S KEPT HIS 34-YEAR MARRIAGE TO WIFE KORIE STRONG

WATCH: Dolly Parton: ‘I pray a lot and God's been really good to me'

Fox News looked back on Parton's history speaking about God in public. "I pray a lot and God's been really good to me," she said in March. In 2018, Parton said that music is "everything to me."

"It's my gift, it's my joy, it's my job," she continued. 

Parton met Carl Dean outside the Wishy Washy Laundromat in Nashville on her first day in the city in 1964, when she was 18. They married two years later, on May 30, 1966, and remained together for nearly six decades until Dean’s death in 2025.

After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs.

DOLLY PARTON'S HUSBAND, CARL DEAN, DEAD AT 82

"I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes."

"I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said.

Also, shortly after Dean's death, Parton told People that she would always keep him close to her heart.

"Ours is a great old love story. Most people don’t stay that close that long. That’s a loss. Nobody can ever know that unless you’ve experienced it yourself. He will always be in my heart and in my memories," she said.

Speaking to Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that part of the reason she believes their marriage lasted as long as it did was because she kept it private.

WATCH: Dolly Parton shares the secret to her long-time marriage

"The fact that he's not in show business at all, so we're not in competition on that. We don't have to deal with it. He's kind of a homebody. He loves working on the farm. He loves workin' on his tractors and his trucks and all that. He was in asphalt paving for years and then he went into kinda doin' some real estate. But he don't wanna be in the spotlight, but he's very proud of, and for me," she said at the time.

"When I first won an award, when we first married in '66... he just started taking clothes off before we even got out of the building. Before we got to the car, he had that bowtie off from that tuxedo. Had that shirt, jacket off and he said, 'I want you to be successful. Do whatever you want to do, but leave me out of this. I ain't doing any more of these things, so don't ask me.' So I never did it," Parton said.

Shortly after Dead died, Parton told the Associated Press that she "truly believe[s] that I’m going to see him again someday."

Parton built a seven-decade career as a singer, songwriter, actress, author, businesswoman and philanthropist, winning 11 Grammy Awards and becoming one of country music’s most enduring stars.

Beyond music, she created Dollywood, founded the Imagination Library and brought her larger-than-life personality to films including "9 to 5" and "Steel Magnolias."

In 2025, Parton spoke to People about how she was able to not only maintain a country music career, but crossover to Hollywood successfully and find the time for her charitable efforts.

"I don’t try to tell other people how to do it, how to be, but I know who I am. I’m a star to everybody but me. I’m just a working girl. I always just say that I’m a workhorse that looks like a show horse," she said at the time.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’m at that point in my life where I just want to be able to do good things that can be carried on. I’m proud of my legacy so far, and I hope to just continue to do things that might be of use to other people," Parton added.

In 2022, Parton said part of the reason she found the time to do the things she loved was because she didn't sleep much.

"I don’t need a whole lot of sleep," the singer insisted to Insider. "I go to bed pretty early, but even if I’ve been up late – it’s just kind of like a little clock inside of me that says, ‘It’s 3 o’clock!’"

"I do some of my best work there, but I get enough sleep. I don’t require as much sleep as a lot of other people do. That’s kind of a Parton family trait," she continued.

After Parton turned 77 in 2023, she spoke to Insider about how she viewed getting older.

The singer said she's come to terms with the idea that "wisdom comes with age, and you can't stop the aging process, nor the numbers."

DOLLY PARTON SAYS SHE’D ‘RATHER BE’ IN HER 70S THAN BE YOUNG AGAIN: ‘I MEAN THIS FROM THE BOTTOM OF MY HEART’

"Honestly — and I mean this from the bottom of my heart — when I see young people today and I see what they're going to have to go through, especially in this day and time, I would honestly rather be this age than that age," Parton explained.

The legendary singer acknowledged she's no different from "everyone (who) would like to stay 35 forever," but she doesn't spend her life thinking about her age and doesn't let it get in the way of her doing what she wants.

"The way I live, the way I work, the way I feel, I'm going to make every moment count," Parton said. "I may live to be 100 or I may die tomorrow, but whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything."

"As long as I stay healthy, the numbers shouldn't matter. I don't feel my age, I don't work my age, I don't think my age and, hopefully, I don't look my age," she noted.

Just before her 80th birthday this year, Parton told People that she felt like she was "just getting started."

item.title: Eating less of common ingredient early in life may slash cancer risk decades later
item.description: Researchers found that early-life sugar rationing in post-war Britain correlated with lower cancer risk and slower aging roughly 50 years later.
item.content:encoded:
Limiting sugar consumption during the first 1,000 days of life, from conception through a child’s second birthday, may result in slower biological aging and a lower risk of cancer up to five decades later.

A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences investigated how early-life sugar intake influences health in adulthood, examining data from over 64,000 participants in the UK Biobank born between 1951 and 1956.

The researchers leveraged a natural experiment from post-war Britain, when sugar rationing ended in September 1953.

DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'

After rationing ended, average daily sugar consumption across the U.K. nearly doubled — from about 41 grams to 80 grams — while consumption of other major foods remained stable, according to historical National Food Survey data cited in the study.

People exposed to sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days of life were compared to those who were conceived after the policy ended. Researchers then examined cancer outcomes recorded about five decades later.

They found that people who spent more of their early lives under sugar rationing had lower rates of several cancers in adulthood, including liver, rectal, lung, prostate and breast cancers.

People exposed to early sugar limits also had longer leukocyte telomeres — protective caps on chromosomes that tend to shorten with age — equivalent to about two fewer years of biological aging. They also had lower levels of Granzyme B, a protein associated with long-term immune activation and inflammation.

EATING COMMON DAIRY FOOD EVERY DAY MAY SLOW BIOLOGICAL AGING, STUDY SUGGESTS

The study’s authors identified two key pathways that could explain these long-term benefits: a biological imprint and a persistent behavioral habit.

Five decades after rationing ended, adults who spent their earliest days under sugar restrictions were still consuming less sugar and eating healthier, more varied diets.

Experts said the findings add to ongoing research into how early diet may influence long-term health, though further research is needed to confirm the connection.

"What surprised me most was how persistent the effects were," study author Weilong Zhang of the University of Cambridge told Fox News Digital.

POPULAR DAILY DRINKING HABIT COULD NEARLY TRIPLE RISK OF DEADLY CANCER, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

"We might expect childhood diet to matter for health, but differences in sugar exposure during just the first 1,000 days were still reflected in people's diets and biological markers roughly five decades later."

"This suggests that early life may be an especially important period not only for biological development, but also for establishing long-lasting food preferences."

Dr. Brian Slomovitz, deputy director of the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, described the research as an "excellent hypothesis-generating study."

"Sugar consumption is something that we have been worrying about ... most importantly, inflammation, and how inflammation can lead to some cancers," Slomovitz, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

High sugar intake has been linked to metabolic disruption, insulin resistance and chronic inflammation, which may contribute to disease risk, according to Dr. Marc Siegel, senior medical analyst for Fox News.

Siegel said the lower cancer rates were consistent with the possibility that less early sugar exposure and healthier later-life diets played a role.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

However, outside oncologists note that natural experiments from decades past come with inherent research limitations.

"We're talking about the 1950s, so clearly there are some biases in data collection," Slomovitz noted. "Secondly, the numbers are very, very, very low. Of all the cancers, most of them had [fewer] than 100 cases ... to show a 70% decrease, I think is probably an ambitious conclusion."

The doctor also pointed out that while obesity-driven cancers align with metabolic pathways, other findings in the paper — such as reduced lung cancer risk — are traditionally tied to external factors like smoking rather than dietary sugar.

The researchers noted that, as a natural experiment rather than a randomized trial, the study could not rule out all other postwar factors.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, the UK Biobank is not fully representative of the broader British population, and the researchers could not determine how much of the effect reflected early biological changes versus healthier diets maintained in adulthood.

Zhang cautioned against overinterpreting the findings as a reason for extreme dietary measures.

"I would not interpret our study as saying that parents should eliminate sugar completely," he said. "Rather, our findings support existing recommendations to limit added sugar, particularly during pregnancy and early childhood."

item.title: Rams' Sean McVay reacts to wild college football controversy: 'Feel like I took a freakin' gummy'
item.description: Sean McVay said he "can't even comprehend" the college football eligibility chaos as SEC and Big Ten block former NFL players from returning.
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay has one way to view the current college football landscape.

Tight end Dae’Quan Wright was expected to become the first-ever player to go from an NFL roster back to an NCAA roster on Wednesday. Wright, who was waived by the Cleveland Browns just two days ago, was reportedly set to reunite with his old Ole Miss coach, Lane Kiffin, at LSU for this upcoming college season.

But hours after he cleared waivers, Wright and the rest of the college football world saw the SEC and Big Ten, which will soon be joined by the ACC and Big 12, create new guidelines for eligibility that would prevent players like Wright who have participated in professional sports from reentering college athletics.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

This came after Wright and other players were granted injunctions or temporary restraining orders allowing them to play this upcoming college season. And most of the lawsuits stem from the NCAA’s new guidelines, which give players five years to play five seasons.

McVay was asked about the college controversy on Tuesday during his press session at training camp. He didn’t even hear the full question, but his reaction said it all.

"Yeah, I can’t even comprehend this stuff," McVay explained. "It’s wild. I don’t know enough about it other than the fact that guys that can be in NFL camps, if it doesn’t go down for them, they can go back college."

McVay put it even more bluntly.

"I feel like I took a freakin’ gummy," McVay said, per the Los Angeles Times.

COLLEGE ATHLETICS' LATEST MESS: COURT ORDERS SAY ATHLETES CAN PLAY, BUT SEC AND BIG TEN READY TO FIGHT

Under the new policies set by the SEC and Big Ten, any athlete that has signed with a pro team in the NFL, declared for the NFL Draft or participated in any type of professional training camp will be ineligible for conference competition.

Attorney Ryan Downton, who represents a number of players trying to get back into the college landscape, told OutKick’s Trey Wallace on Tuesday night that they are currently "working on a legal strategy" on how to move forward against both the NCAA and the respective conferences that enacted the new guidelines.

"The SEC’s actions put the NCAA in contempt of multiple court orders," Downton told OutKick-Fox News on Tuesday night. "It is cartel-like conduct when NCAA conferences attempt to create their own spur of the moment rules in response to Courts enjoining those same rules at the NCAA level."

Wright is among a group of former college football players who were all granted a temporary restraining order by a judge in Louisiana. He is among several athletes from the 2022 high school class that tried capitalizing on the NCAA’s five-year eligibility guidelines, which was unanimously approved by the NCAA Division I Cabinet in June.

OutKick’s Trey Wallace contributed to this report.

item.title: Washington Redskins gear is available to fans in the Commanders' team shop at stadium and online
item.description: The Washington Commanders are selling throwback jerseys and T-shirts bearing the Redskins name the franchise discarded in 2020 as racist or offensive.
item.content:encoded:
The Washington Redskins name and iconic logo that the NFL team in the nation's capital abandoned in 2020 is back in a manner of speaking. It's on full display and for sale in the team's current merchandise shop.

Although the gear bearing the Redskins name is rare and limited to a Mitchell & Ness throwback line of T-shirts or jerseys bearing the name of former players who played with the Redskins name and helmet insignia, it is indeed for sale.

Anyone can go to the brick-and-mortar store at Northwest Stadium or online and buy, for example, an Art Monk T-shirt bearing the Pro Football Hall Fame receiver's likeness in his old uniform and in his Redskins helmet.

TAYLOR HEINICKE RETIRES FROM THE NFL WITH A FAREWELL SALUTE TO THE WASHINGTON REDSKINS

The back of that T-shirt is emblazoned with "Washington Redskins" and Monk's career statistics and records. The shirt costs $49.99.

For the same price, fans can purchase a Sean Taylor T-Shirt with the likeness of the former safety in his Redskins uniform before he was tragically slain in 2007. Like Monk, Taylor played for the Redskins, not the Washington Commanders.

Taylor's retired No. 21 jersey, complete with the Redskins name on the front and a 75th anniversary Washington Redskins patch, is available for $114.99.

The interesting thing about this is the franchise is marketing this gear emblazoned with Washington Redskins script and logos as Commanders gear.

The jersey, for example, is described as a Sean Taylor Black Washington Commanders Retired Player Name & Number Mesh Top – even though the Commanders nickname does not appear on the jersey.

NFL AND CONGRESS DISCUSS RETURN OF THE WASHINGTON REDSKINS LOGO

This is what happens when an NFL franchise builds a long and storied history as the Washington Redskins from 1937 to 2019, then decides the Redskins nickname is racist or otherwise offensive under pressure from liberal fans, some Native American groups and sponsors.

The Washington Commanders, as they're known now, have vowed never to return to the Redskins nickname.

Current owner Josh Harris said in September 2023 that he understands the nostalgia for the former name but that "there was a portion of our fan base that felt disrespected by the former name."

So why, if the Redskins name is bothersome, are the Commanders selling Redskins merchandise? And why are they later this season wearing an alternate helmet with a spear piercing the W insignia, much like the old feathered arrow helmet the Redskins wore in the 1960s?

The spear that is part of the so-called "Raise Hail" alternate uniform is an obvious reach at Redskins nostalgia.

The gear in the team gift shop is being made available to keep the old trademark in commercial use, according to WUSA9 in Washington.

"We are required to maintain the marks in commercial usage so that marks remain under franchise control," a club spokesman told the television station.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

A trademark may be deemed abandoned if its use is discontinued with intent not resume use. The Lanham Act says that three consecutive years of nonuse is prima facie evidence of abandonment.

The statutory standard also requires "bona fide use … in the ordinary course of trade," rather than merely token sales made solely to reserve rights.

That might be a problem for the Commanders because their contention is that these Redskins items are sold on a limited availability.

It should be noted that there are Native American groups who believe the Redskins nickname to be indeed racist. But other native individuals, including a Navajo Code Talkers Association leader and a former Blackfeet tribal chairman, have publicly supported retaining the old nickname and the Native-profile logo.

Walter "Blackie" Wetzel, a former chairman of the Blackfeet Tribe and former president of the National Congress of American Indians, helped persuade the club in 1972 to replace its "R" helmet logo with the Native chief helmet portrait most associated with the team.

In a 2002 interview, Wetzel said: "It made us all so proud to have an Indian on a big-time team. It’s only a small group of radicals who oppose those names. Indians are proud of Indians."

item.title: Missouri grandma ordered to stop serving free breakfasts refuses to back down, 'They are my family'
item.description: Kathy Kite says she won't stop serving free breakfast in Harrisburg, Missouri, despite a health department letter saying she needs a permit.
item.content:encoded:
A Missouri grandmother says she was frightened she could end up in legal trouble after county health officials told her to stop serving free homemade breakfasts without a permit, but she told Fox News Digital she has no intention of giving up the morning tradition that brings her tiny community together.

"I'm not gonna stop providing for my community," Kathy Kite of Harrisburg, Missouri, told Fox News Digital in an interview Tuesday. "I wouldn't stop feeding my children, I wouldn't stop feeding my family. I'm not gonna stop feeding my community cause they are my family… This is bigger than that. It's about love and appreciation because they appreciate what I do."

Kite has been cooking free breakfasts for her neighbors and friends since May. In July, she received a letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department that said she needed to obtain a food permit or face possible legal action.

YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE

"I got the letter in July, it upset me, because I didn't understand what I was doing wrong," Kite said. "It hurt my feelings, and it upset me because I knew at that point I was afraid I was gonna go to jail because the letter stated that if I didn't stop making breakfast for my community, that I was facing fines and jail, and so I posted it on Facebook and people responded." 

The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department denied that their letter threatened jail time, in comments to Fox News Digital.

Kite said that after the local gas station where she works stopped serving breakfast following COVID, regular customers kept asking for it, so she invited them to her home and began cooking breakfast for them herself.

Kite said that what began as an early-morning breakfast for a few regulars quickly spread across the town of fewer than 300 people. More residents began stopping by for coffee and breakfast, staying to talk about farming, the weather and childhood memories. The growing sense of community motivated her to wake up even earlier to cook, and soon local mothers were bringing their children by for breakfast before school.

ORTHODOX JEW ASKS SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CASE AFTER CITY ALLEGEDLY TARGETED HIS HOME PRAYER GROUP

Kite said the letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department says that she must install a commercial kitchen in her home.

"In order for me to comply with what they're asking, I would have to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to have a commercial kitchen in my home," Kite said. "I live in a 115-year-old home. It's a beautiful home. I'm not gonna jeopardize the integrity of my home to put a commercial kitchen in to make some free burritos."

She said she would welcome city officials into her home so they could see firsthand what she is doing.

"Come have a burrito. I'm [not] doing anything wrong. I don't, I just, I can't understand. Come to my home, see my home, and see that my home is not dirty," Kite said. "I don't have cats. I'm not making people sick. I am just a grandma cooking a meal for my friends and family and enjoying life."

The Goldwater Institute sent a letter Thursday to the Boone County health department demanding they answer questions by Friday about their legal reasoning. The group said that no lawsuit has been filed to date, but it is on the table.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Dave Roland, Goldwater Institute's director of allied litigation, said, "Kathy’s story is a textbook example of bureaucracy run amok. Citizens should not be required to get the government’s permission before offering passers-by some coffee and a bite to eat while they socialize. The government exists to protect this sort of neighborly kindness, not to punish it."

The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department told Fox News Digital that food permits are not required when providing food for family and friends, but a permit is required when providing food to the public, citing the Missouri food code.

"At the time the complaint was received, Ms. Kite’s home had an open sign, tip jar, advertised food on social media and a sign in her yard — all things that are typically associated with a food establishment," the spokesperson said.

"No citations or cease-and-desist orders were issued," the statement continued. "We also did not threaten jail time. We sent a letter to Ms. Kite following a complaint we received that food served in her establishment made someone ill. Our role in public health is to work with food establishments to promote safe food practices and prevent food-borne illnesses. There are safe, allowable ways to provide homemade food to the community with and without a food permit. We regularly work together with individuals and businesses who want to provide free food to the community."

item.description: In celebration of National Dog Day, Lord Jameson's founder says the MAHA movement should extend to pets with organic, whole-food treats free of artificial additives.
item.content:encoded:
It's National Dog Day, and one dog treat creator thinks dogs should be included in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative, which emphasizes whole, nutrient-dense foods.

"We have never used anything artificial," Sarah Goldberger, New York-based founder and CEO of organic dog treat company Lord Jameson, told Fox News Digital. 

"We've never used fake food coloring. We've never used fake flavoring. All of our bright, beautiful colors come from real fruits and vegetables."

CHEAP, HEALTHY FOOD IS REJECTED BY MOST AMERICANS EVEN AS MAHA MOVEMENT PUSHES IT

Since becoming an official federal initiative in February 2025, the MAHA Commission has promoted a greater focus on whole, nutrient-dense foods while calling for reductions in refined carbohydrates, added sugars and certain artificial additives.

Goldberger believes those nutritional priorities will "translate into the pet space."

"My hope is that as a brand, we can inspire other pet brands to make better choices to really impact the lives and the health and wellness of dogs," she said.

Goldberger started Lord Jameson in 2019, inspired by her late dog, Jameson, after noticing what she described as a void in the market for healthier dog treats.

HERE'S WHY DOGS DON'T NEED 'HUMAN FOOD,' SAYS VIRGINIA VETERINARIAN: 'NO REASON FOR IT'

"Jameson had gone through a pretty serious medical issue, and the medication he was being given actually created toxicity in his body," Goldberger said. 

"So we started working with a homeopathic vet, and we were reminded of the power of plant-based medicine. A lot of the formulas, especially in our wellness products, are meant to serve dogs during a time of needed healing with plant-based products, more herbs and botanicals."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

When she set out to create the brand, Goldberger said she surveyed more than 1,000 pet parents and found that many reported their dogs had allergies or sensitivities to various animal proteins, preservatives and food colorings.

Goldberger said she wanted to offer treats made with "completely clean ingredients, organic, gluten-free, no preservatives, no toxins, no artificial colors or flavors."

Despite not using preservatives, the treats have an 18-month shelf life, which Goldberger said is "very difficult to achieve in production" and is "another key selling point for us."

Lord Jameson, Goldberger said, has "truly reimagined what dog treats can be and should be."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

She said she eats the treats herself and even puts them in her children's lunchboxes.

They've been a hit with pet owners for a variety of reasons, including what Goldberger described as their effect on dogs' digestive systems.

"As a dog mom myself, I know the frustration when you go to the store, you buy food or a treat, you bring it home and all of a sudden they have diarrhea," she said. 

"Because we're using whole-food ingredients and no preservatives, you're going to get a nice firm poop after they eat. It sounds funny to say, but this is something you'll see in a lot of our reviews."

Goldberger also said the treats can be suitable for some dogs with colitis, diabetes or other specialized dietary needs.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Lord Jameson has since launched a line of "protein-inspired" flavors as part of its Love Puffs line, made with organic sorghum, a whole grain that contains protein and fiber.

Another feature that sets Lord Jameson apart, Goldberger said, is that the brand is "completely vertically integrated," with its manufacturing operations, including its kitchen, warehouse and fulfillment center, based in Boulder, Colorado.

"We've had no price increase for three or four years, no issues with any tariffs because everything is sourced primarily in North America," Goldberger said.

Lord Jameson treats are sold at 5,500 independent pet retailers in the United States, as well as at some grocery stores, and are available internationally in four countries.

Kelly McGreal of Fox News Digital contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump’s Economic D-Day can hammer Iran, but will Tehran ever surrender?
item.description: Scott Bessent's "Economic D-Day" Iran sanctions echo World War II's D-Day, but history shows punishing Tehran and forcing surrender are vastly different.
item.content:encoded:
I lived in Europe for years, studying World War II not only in books but on the ground, walking battlefields and cemeteries and listening to veterans who had fought their way across the continent.

For America and our European allies, D-Day was an all-in fight. Survival was at stake. There was no ambiguity about the enemy or the objective.

So, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called his new maximum-pressure campaign against Iran an "Economic D-Day," a term he used this week, one question immediately came to mind:

Where is V-E Day?

The real D-Day came on June 6, 1944. Nazi Germany did not surrender until May 8, 1945. That was 11 months later.

D-Day was not victory. It began the final campaign toward victory.

Bessent deserves credit for launching something much more ambitious than another sanctions package. The administration calls it Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to sever Iran’s remaining economic lifelines in shipping, aviation, technology, gold and digital assets, with secondary sanctions threatened against foreign enablers. About 60 individuals, entities and vessels were targeted in the opening round.

TRUMP THREATENS 'UNPRECEDENTED' ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES FOR ANY NATION AIDING IRAN

And there is an important difference from President Donald Trump’s first-term "maximum pressure" campaign: the U.S. Navy.

Previous sanctions made Iranian oil hard to finance, insure and sell. Today, unlike the first-term campaign, the administration is pairing financial pressure with what AP reports is a Navy-enforced blockade of Iranian ports.

The administration hopes to deepen a decline already evident in Iranian oil shipments to China. Iranian oil shipments to China fell to about 534,000 barrels a day in August, down from 823,000 in July and from a 2026 peak of roughly 1.58 million. Chinese refiners are scrambling for alternative supplies.

Iran is hurting badly.

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

Its currency has been battered, and its infrastructure has been damaged. Iran’s own Statistical Centre reports annual inflation reached 88% in July, with food prices up 128% from a year earlier. The regime worries that additional hardship could trigger renewed domestic unrest.

All of this proves Bessent can make Iran poorer. It does not prove he can make Iran surrender.

History demonstrates the difference.

Treasury Secretary Jack Lew testified that the sanctions preceding the 2015 nuclear agreement cost Iran more than $160 billion in oil revenue after 2012, with exports down 60% and the rial down by half.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES

But sanctions did not produce Iranian capitulation. They brought Tehran to the negotiating table. Iran retained uranium enrichment while accepting restrictions and inspections in exchange for sanctions relief.

Trump tried differently after withdrawing from the nuclear agreement in 2018. His first maximum-pressure campaign again inflicted enormous damage, yet Iran never accepted Washington’s broader demands on nuclear activities, missiles and regional behavior before he left office.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS OPPOSE THE IRAN WAR, SEE PROLONGED COMMITMENT

Outcomes are what matters. Government studies of sanctions have repeatedly found it easier to measure economic punishment than to demonstrate that the punishment produced the desired foreign-policy outcome. GAO also found sanctions work better when they are multilateral and when the target depends on the countries imposing them.

Treasury can count barrels Iran cannot sell, dollars Tehran cannot collect and banks it can no longer use.

Those numbers tell us how much Iran is hurting.

They do not tell us whether Iran is surrendering.

There is also something unusual about the regime Bessent is trying to coerce.

Ordinary Iranians certainly do not welcome economic misery. They have repeatedly protested inflation, unemployment and declining living standards.

But the Islamic Republic’s revolutionary leadership has spent nearly five decades building political legitimacy around resistance to foreign pressure, sacrifice and self-reliance. The regime’s so-called "resistance economy" was built to help Iran endure sanctions, not capitulate to end them.

Economic coercion assumes the target eventually concludes that continued suffering is worse than concession. Iran’s revolutionary rulers have spent nearly half a century teaching themselves that concession to America can be worse than suffering.

Then there is China.

Beijing purchases more than 80% of Iran’s shipped oil and has already rejected Washington’s new sanctions strategy.

Iranian crude has survived previous sanctions through Chinese independent refiners, shadow tankers, disguised cargo origins and transactions conducted in Chinese currency.

Yet the administration initially spared major Chinese banks, reportedly to avoid disrupting the global financial system, as Trump and Xi Jinping prepare to meet.

Washington sanctioned a smaller Chinese bank once before, cutting off Bank of Kunlun in 2012 for handling Iranian banks’ money. Threatening a systemically important state bank is a different order of confrontation.

How can maximum pressure on Iran be maximum if Washington is unwilling to impose maximum pressure on Iran’s largest economic lifeline?

China does not have to restore normal Iranian commerce. It only has to permit enough oil purchases, financial transactions and sanctions evasion to keep Tehran breathing.

Its strategy can be brutally simple: absorb the contraction, repress unrest, keep commerce flowing through China, and keep Hormuz dangerous enough that Americans share the pain.

Iran doesn’t need to outfight Trump. It needs to outlast him. That turns Bessent’s Economic D-Day into an endurance contest, and endurance depends on the costs borne by both sides.

And America is paying.

The Iran war has already depleted scarce Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors, with a CSIS analysis estimating reductions of 65% and 38%, respectively. Those are munitions we may need in a conflict with China, the same conflict that already forced the Japan-homeported USS George Washington to divert to the Middle East, relieving USS Abraham Lincoln after a deployment beyond 250 days.

The political cost is rising too. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll finds only 31% of Americans support the Iran war, while 83% believe it will last a long time. Washington also has less room to cushion another energy shock: the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to roughly 290 million barrels, its lowest level since November 1982, after repeated emergency releases. If Hormuz deteriorates further, that safety net is much thinner.

Iran’s leaders can read an election calendar.

The contest, therefore, is not simply whether Bessent can bankrupt Iran. It is whether Iran’s economy breaks before America’s political patience does.

Secretary Bessent may indeed have launched an impressive Economic D-Day.

But D-Day was never the objective.

Victory was.

The Allies knew what victory meant on June 6, 1944: allies committed to the campaign, a strategy for reaching Germany, and an unmistakable end state.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Before committing to this costly war’s next phase against an adversary that has spent 47 years learning to endure American pressure, the administration owes Americans basic answers.

What does victory over Iran mean? How long will it take? What price are we prepared to pay? And what happens if Tehran simply refuses to surrender?

If Economic D-Day cannot answer those questions, America may not have found a way out of another forever war.

It may simply have found another way to fight one.

item.title: AOC says ‘Woke 1 was crazy,’ but Democrats still owe voters an explanation
item.description: New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's "Woke 1" label lets Democrats compartmentalize 2020 progressive politics without a reckoning.
item.content:encoded:
"Woke 1 was crazy."

New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently borrowed the phrase from New York City Councilman Chi Ossé to describe the politics of 2020. "Woke 1" gives Democrats a convenient way to put ideas such as defunding the police and abolishing prisons in the past. That was then. This is now. There’s a psychological term for this kind of separation: compartmentalization.

Consider how compartmentalization works in ordinary life. A married man can have a wife and children at home and a girlfriend on the side, keeping the two lives separate enough that he rarely confronts the contradiction. Compartmentalization allows us to separate conflicting parts of our lives rather than reconcile them.

ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ SHRUGS OFF PAST 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS, JOKING 'WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY'

That appears to be what Democrats are trying to do with 2020. There is the Democratic Party of 2020, when progressive ideas that once sat outside the mainstream suddenly gained influence. Then there is the Democratic Party of 2026, talking about affordability, economic populism and winning back voters who recoiled from the cultural politics of the past several years. "Woke 1" puts a neat dividing line between them. Changing your mind requires confronting what you once believed. Compartmentalization doesn’t.

Many political beliefs in 2020 became tests of character. They didn’t just say what you believed. They said what kind of person you were. If people you dismissed six years ago turned out to have a point, you have more to reconsider than a policy. Maybe you were too certain. Maybe you mistook disagreement for prejudice.

MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS

Or you can call the whole thing "Woke 1."

Except 2020 didn’t simply happen to the Democratic Party. Politicians embraced ideas, activists pushed them, and institutions decided which arguments deserved a hearing and which could be dismissed. People who challenged the prevailing views sometimes paid a price for it. Calling all of this "Woke 1" makes those choices sound like the product of a strange moment everyone has since outgrown.

AOC'S ATTEMPT TO DISMISS 'WOKE 1' AS 'CRAZY' DRAWS CRITICISM FROM LEFT-LEANING OUTLETS

If Democrats now reject positions they embraced or tolerated in 2020, voters can reasonably expect an explanation. The key question is whether Democrats changed their minds or discovered that voters had.

There is nothing shameful about changing your mind. Real change requires connecting what you believed then with what you believe now and acknowledging where you got it wrong. Without that reckoning, voters are left to wonder whether the beliefs changed or the incentives did.

DNC’S 192-PAGE AUTOPSY SOUNDS LIKE BAD THERAPY. DEMOCRATS STILL HAVE A BIG PROBLEM

Democrats can compartmentalize 2020. Voters don’t have to.

A candidate may regard a six-year-old position as ancient history, but an opponent can revive it with an old interview, campaign questionnaire or social media post. "That was then" invites an obvious response: Yes, but that was you.

DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CALLED FOR MASS RELEASE OF CRIMINALS DURING PRISON ABOLITION WEBINAR

Democrats aren’t unique in doing this. Every political party finds ways to distance itself from positions that become inconvenient. But 2020 poses a particular problem because so many political beliefs became tied to moral identity. Giving up a position can feel like admitting something about yourself, not just admitting that a policy was wrong.

There is a way out. Democrats could acknowledge that 2020 drew attention to genuine problems while also producing bad ideas. They could concede that some rhetoric went too far and that some people were treated unfairly for challenging the prevailing consensus. That doesn’t require abandoning concern about racism, police misconduct or inequality. It requires admitting that you can feel morally certain and still be wrong.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The familiar Democratic argument is about whether the party should move left or toward the center. "Woke 1" raises a more interesting question: Before Democrats decide where they are going, can they explain what they now think about where they have been?

"Woke 1 was crazy" sounds like a confession. But it isn’t quite one. A confession names what you got wrong. Compartmentalization puts it somewhere you no longer have to look.

item.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Abdul El-Sayed’s wealth-tax fantasy could wreck the Michigan economy
item.description: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed frames extreme wealth as an existential threat, but critics warn his tax plan could trigger an exodus of top earners from Michigan.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is tackling a new national crisis: the excess of money held by some tragically wealthy citizens.

In his interview this week with Fox News’ Jesse Watters, the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate not only reaffirmed his call for a wealth tax, but suggested that wealthy people really do not have much use for money that would be better left to the public.

El-Sayed needs money. A lot of money. He has called for massive new programs to fund Medicare-for-All, reparations, roads and other programs promised to Michigan voters. He is only the latest Democratic leader to support a wealth tax, which would, in my opinion, be unconstitutional at the federal level and disastrous at the state level.

ABDUL EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PAST STATEMENTS ON SHARIA LAW AND WHITE SUPREMACY, TAXING THE RICH

Earlier in the week, El-Sayed expressed full support for a wealth tax, including on non-billionaires. He declared on a podcast: "I also think we got to start taxing wealth for people who now have over $100 million. I mean at that point like what are gonna even do with more money?"

Figures such as Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., have also called for a wealth tax on millionaires, not just billionaires. As some of us predicted, the use of billionaires was simply a strategic and political framing. Once politicians succeed in opening up this untapped wealth to taxation, they will gradually work down the tax rolls as they acquire a windfall in new revenue.

PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST

I discuss the tax in my book, "Rage and the Republic," as an example of the "eat-the-rich" politics used by demagogues from ancient Athens to the French Revolution. Politicians seek to divide a population into "haves" and "have-nots" with the promise that citizens can have it all. Much of what El-Sayed said is ripped from the pages of figures such as Huey Long and his "Share Our Wealth" campaigns of the 1930s.

In his Fox News interview, El-Sayed reaffirmed his call for a wealth tax, adding: "The question ultimately is, ‘Do you want to drive on good roads, or would you rather have a billionaire make a second billion?’ That’s what Mike Rogers wants. That’s why Donald Trump wants. Apparently, that’s what you want. I think the people in Michigan want something different."

While El-Sayed and his wife reported $686,069 in income in 2025, they would not be subject to the wealth tax. It would apply to those with $100 million or more in property and other forms of wealth.

EL-SAYED IN THE HOT SEAT FOR ANOTHER FOREIGN RENTAL PROPERTY, NEARLY $300K IN ADDITIONAL INCOME

El-Sayed appears to conflate or confuse wealth taxes and income taxes in the interview. He told Watters, "If we tax you at 7%, you’re still going to make what? A cool $30 million off your billion dollars? I think that’s OK, they’re going to be OK, Jesse."

El-Sayed did not explain his assumptions. He may have been assuming that a $1 billion fortune generates a 10% annual return: $100 million in gains, less a hypothetical 7% wealth tax of $70 million, leaving $30 million. Whether such a return, tax rate and tax base are realistic is a separate question.

There is a great difference between a wealth tax and an income tax. The wealthy have already paid taxes on much of their wealth. Indeed, they pay income taxes when the money is earned and pay taxes on any profits from that money when it is invested in stock or property. A wealth tax is an additional tax on all that you own, from homes to boats to art.

At a 7% tax on wealth for those worth $100,000,000, the wealthy would pay an additional $7,000,000 every year in Michigan beyond their income taxes.

SIX DIFFERENT WAYS THAT PROVE THE WEALTHY PAY A LOT MORE THAN THEIR ‘FAIR SHARE’

If a government imposed a 7% annual tax on $100 million in net wealth, the annual liability would be $7 million—though El-Sayed has not released a detailed proposal establishing that rate or threshold. In Michigan, they would also face the state income tax of 4.25% and a 6% corporate tax on their businesses. If the wealth tax is added to an income tax, that would be in addition to the 37% top federal income tax rate.

Again, the wealth tax would continue to apply each year to what an individual owns in the form of cars, homes and other property, regardless of whether income declines.

AOC TRIPLES DOWN, CLAIMS AMERICAN REVOLUTION WAS AGAINST 'THE BILLIONAIRES OF THEIR TIME'

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., drove this point home when she ran for president in 2020, taunting the wealthy that she was coming for "your Rembrandts, your stock portfolio, your diamonds and your yachts."

While some states are actively considering a wealth tax, many of us view it as unconstitutional under the federal system. The federal government secured the right to tax individuals in 1913, but the 16th Amendment only approved income taxes.

DAVID MARCUS: HOW DEMOCRATS SNEAKED IN REPARATIONS, AND HOW THEY'LL PROTECT THEM

This is why many of these same politicians are promising a hostile takeover of the Supreme Court by either eliminating the Court or packing it with an instant liberal majority. Once packed, the Court could greenlight a variety of unconstitutional measures.

Years ago, Harvard professor Michael Klarman laid out a radical agenda to change the system to guarantee Republicans will never win another election. However, he warned that "the Supreme Court could strike down everything I just described." Therefore, the Court must be packed in advance to allow these changes to occur.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM?

Even if states like Michigan are allowed to do this, it will result in the same exodus that is currently unfolding in California, where possibly trillions of dollars in jobs and revenue have already been lost due to the mere threat of wealth taxes. That is why figures like Khanna and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., are calling for a national wealth tax, leaving the wealthy nowhere to go but out of the country.

This is precisely what socialist governments like France under François Mitterrand attempted in the last century, with disastrous results that tanked the economy and forced a rapid retreat from such policies.

THE ONLY MAP YOU NEED TO SEE AS CALIFORNIA'S BILLIONAIRE TAX FIGHT HEATS UP

As Michigan struggles to secure new businesses and jobs, El-Sayed is embracing the same policies that would decapitate the top of its tax base. While repeating the mantra that the wealthy are "not paying their fair share," the top 10% pays more in federal income taxes than the bottom 90% combined. In 2023, the top 1% paid an estimated 38.4% of all federal individual income taxes.

El-Sayed has proven himself a gifted politician. He juxtaposes concrete benefits like new roads with the image of unused wealth among top earners. The fact is that Michigan will have fewer roads if it chases away top earners with their businesses and jobs.

Like Long, who referred to "our wealth" being held by the rich, El-Sayed portrays the property of the wealthy as rightfully belonging to the people, promising that if we "put a tax on wealth it would return a lot of that money back into public use."

El-Sayed has perfected the "eat-the-rich" pitch by portraying the wealthy as virtual Scrooge McDucks who accumulate unused wealth as a type of vanity project. He has struck out at "people who have accumulated so much wealth that your money makes money." That is also called investments that power the economy — and when your "money makes money," it is taxed as income.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Nevertheless, El-Sayed is waging the same class war as other rising figures in the Democratic Party, denouncing "extreme wealth" as "an existential threat to our economy and our democracy, and it demands a crisis-level response."

The real crisis is unfolding as candidates like El-Sayed are promising trillions in new programs while promising to make the rich pay for them. As with Warren, their property is being portrayed as rightfully belonging to the public.

The problem is that both wealth and the wealthy are mobile, and few are likely to stick around for El-Sayed’s people’s paradise in Michigan.
